summary.text: Ampère's circuital law relates the circulation of a magnetic field around a closed loop to the electric current passing through that loop.
It was inspired by Ørsted's 1820 finding that an electric current makes a magnetic field, and in 1865 Maxwell extended it with a displacement current term.
The original law holds only for steady currents, so Maxwell's correction is needed when electric fields change in time; the result is one of Maxwell's equations.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Ampère's circuital law (often just called Ampère's law, and now and then named Oersted's law) relates how a magnetic field circulates around a closed loop to the current that flows through the loop. In 1865 Maxwell widened it to cover currents that change over time. The equation that came out of this, often known as the Ampère–Maxwell law, counts among Maxwell's equations, which form the foundation of classical electromagnetism.

paragraphs.heading: Ørsted's compass
paragraphs.text: Until the early 1800s, electricity and magnetism were thought to be completely separate. That changed in 1820, when the Danish physicist Hans Christian Ørsted found that an electric current has a magnetic effect. A compass needle near a wire carrying current swung to sit at right angles to the wire. In further experiments he showed that the current could affect magnetic poles nearby, that its effect spread outward from the wire, and that it formed a vortex around the wire.

paragraphs.heading: From Ampère to Maxwell
paragraphs.text: Ørsted's discovery set off a wave of research into how electricity and magnetism are related. André-Marie Ampère studied the magnetic force between two wires carrying current and discovered Ampère's force law. In the 1850s James Clerk Maxwell pulled these results and others into a single mathematical law. He published it in 1855 in his paper "On Faraday's Lines of Force", basing it on an analogy with hydrodynamics. In 1865 he extended it to currents that change over time by adding a displacement current term.

paragraphs.heading: What the original law says
paragraphs.text: The original law connects magnetic fields to the currents that produce them. It works in both directions: it can give the magnetic field for a known current, or the current for a known field. But it holds only in magnetostatic situations, meaning steady, continuous currents flowing in closed circuits. When electric fields change over time, the law needs an extra term known as Maxwell's correction.

paragraphs.heading: Loops and surfaces
paragraphs.text: In its integral form, the law adds up the magnetic field along a closed curve, called C. That curve is the edge of a surface, S, which the current passes through. Written with the B field, the total around C is proportional to the total current crossing S. Many surfaces share the same edge, like a soap film on a wire loop that changes shape when you blow on it. In the magnetostatic case it makes no difference which one you pick, so in practice people choose whichever is most convenient.

paragraphs.heading: Free and bound current
paragraphs.text: The current in simple textbook cases, such as the current through a wire or a battery, counts as free current. Bound current arises in bulk materials that can be magnetized or polarized, which all materials can be to some extent. When a material is magnetized, its electrons stay with their atoms but behave as if circling the nucleus in one direction, making a microscopic current. Added together, these act like one large current circulating forever around the magnetized object. The version of the law written with the H field counts only the free current, while the B version counts the total, free plus bound.
